slides.name: 1 · Teacher preparation

params.text:
Ages 9–18  ·  5 minutes  ·  no preparation, no account, no extra materials
Timing  30s scenario  ·  45s vote  ·  75s pairs  ·  75s reveal  ·  30s remember  ·  45s action
You need  this deck on the board. Phones are optional — a show of hands works.

slides.notes:
PURPOSE. Students move from "can you spot AI?" to "what did you declare?" — the first is already unanswerable, the second is entirely in their control.

LIKELY RESPONSES. The most genuinely split vote in the campaign. "Depends what you do next" is the sophisticated answer; ask whoever picks it what "next" involves.

CONNECT TO YOUR OWN POLICY. This is your school’s academic-integrity rules in student language. If you have a written AI policy, name it here — the slide sets up the habit, your policy sets the line.

SEND / YOUNGER LEARNERS. Use a drawing rather than a song. "Who made it?" is easier when the thing is visible and one object.

EXTENSION. Write the declaration line for the last piece of work you handed in. Would you have been comfortable attaching it?

SOURCE. Content Credentials (C2PA) — provenance travelling with the file.

slides.name: 2 · Who really made it?
slides.notes:
SLIDE 1 · TITLE. Up as the class comes in. The question does the work; do not explain it yet.

The full teacher page is the hidden slide before this one — purpose, timing, script, safeguarding, SEND and an extension.

slides.name: 3 · quote

params.text: I typed one sentence. It wrote the song, made the cover and mixed it.

slides.notes:
BEAT 1 · 30 SECONDS.

Keep it neutral. The work in this scenario might be good — that is what makes the question hard. If you imply it is rubbish, there is nothing left to discuss.

slides.name: 4 · Who made it?

params.text: It was your idea. Nobody else would have asked for that.
You started it. Something else finished it.
One sentence is not making something.
It is not finished being made yet.
Choose A, B, C or D. Be ready to say why.

slides.notes:
BEAT 2 · 45 SECONDS. Vote first.

This is the most genuinely split vote in the whole campaign. Take it properly and show the spread.

Ask someone who chose the fourth option to say what "next" would have to involve. They usually arrive at the answer on their own.

slides.name: 5 · statement

params.text: What would you have to add before you would put your name on it?

slides.notes:
BEAT 3 · 75 SECONDS.

Better than "is it yours", because it cannot be answered yes or no. It forces them to name a contribution.

Listen for "changing a few words". Ask whether they would accept that from someone else claiming to have written their favourite song.

slides.name: 6 · "My track. Out now."

params.text: The same claim, with its working shown
one sentence — but nobody else wrote that sentence
you kept them as they came
this is the row that decides the answer
the post does not say any of the above
Modelled on Content Credentials (C2PA) — provenance attached to the file, not guessed from it

slides.notes:
BEAT 4 · 75 SECONDS. Reveal one row at a time.

This is a content credential, rendered as a slide. The real ones ride inside the file and say what tool touched it and when — provenance attached, rather than guessed at afterwards.

THE SHIFT TO MAKE: the interesting question is not "can you tell?" That game is already lost. It is "what did you declare?" — which you control completely.

Row 5 is where authorship actually lives. Row 6 is the one that gets people into trouble, at school and later at work.

slides.name: 7 · What to remember

params.text: Before anyone has to ask you.
Add what only you could add
Your judgement, your experience, your choices.
Be able to explain every choice
If you cannot, it is not finished being made.
Three things, in the order you would use them

slides.notes:
SLIDE 6 · 30 SECONDS. Reveal one at a time. Three is the limit — a fourth rule is a rule nobody remembers.

Numbered rather than bulleted so the order is part of the message, and so nothing here depends on colour to be understood.

slides.name: 8 · Decide what you would declare

params.text: Write the one line you would put underneath it, honestly describing what you did and what the tool did.

slides.notes:
BEAT 5 · 45 SECONDS. One line, in their heads or on paper.

The test that survives contact with the real world: would you be comfortable if the person marking it, or hiring you, could see exactly how it was made?

Not an anti-AI message. A disclosure habit is what lets you use these tools without the question hanging over everything you make.

slides.name: 9 · Two words worth knowing

params.text: The record of where something came from and what happened to it along the way.
Saying plainly what you used and what you did — before anyone has to ask.

slides.notes:
HIDDEN FROM THE SHOW — the brief asks for seven student-facing slides and this is not one of them.

Worth thirty seconds anyway. Both terms are used on the slides this deck shows, and a word nobody defines is a word nobody argues with.

Written for 11–16, not for a policy paper.
